An octopus has no bones, no shell, and very little protection from the many fish, seals, and eels that want to eat it. What it does have is one of the most remarkable disguise systems in the animal world.

Just beneath an octopus's skin lie thousands of tiny sacs of color called chromatophores. Each sac is surrounded by muscles. When the muscles squeeze or relax, the sac opens or closes, changing the color of that spot of skin in less than a second. Some octopuses can also raise small bumps on their skin, making smooth skin look rough like a rock or coral.

What puzzles scientists is that most octopuses are believed to be colorblind. Their eyes have only one type of color-sensing cell, yet they match their surroundings with astonishing accuracy. One possible explanation is that their skin itself contains light-sensing proteins similar to those found in eyes. If so, an octopus may, in a sense, "see" with its skin.

Researchers are still testing this idea. For now, the octopus remains a master of disguise that keeps its biggest secret well hidden.

In 1817, New York governor DeWitt Clinton proposed digging a canal more than 360 miles long, connecting the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo. Many people thought the idea was absurd. At the time, the longest canal in America was less than 30 miles long. Critics mocked the project as "Clinton's Ditch."

Construction took eight years. Workers, many of them Irish immigrants, dug much of the canal by hand with shovels, picks, and horse-drawn plows. Because few American engineers had canal experience, many learned on the job, solving problems as they appeared.

When the Erie Canal opened in 1825, the results silenced most critics. Before the canal, moving a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City cost about $100 and took weeks. Afterward, it cost roughly $10 and took about eight days. Farmers in the Midwest could suddenly sell crops on the East Coast, and New York City grew into the busiest port in the nation.

The "ditch" that people once laughed at had changed the shape of American trade.

Today she is recognized as one of the founders of paleontology, the study of fossils.
